**Ring Out, Wild Bells**
*by Alfred, Lord Tennyson*

Ring out, wild bells, to the wild sky,
　The flying cloud, the frosty light:
　The year is dying in the night;
Ring out, wild bells, and let him die.

Ring out the old, ring in the new,
　Ring, happy bells, across the snow:
　The year is going, let him go;
Ring out the false, ring in the true.

Ring out the grief that saps the mind
　For those that here we see no more;
　Ring out the feud of rich and poor,
Ring in redress to all mankind.

Ring out a slowly dying cause,
　And ancient forms of party strife;
　Ring in the nobler modes of life,
With sweeter manners, purer laws.

Ring out the want, the care, the sin,
　The faithless coldness of the times;
　Ring out, ring out my mournful rhymes
But ring the fuller minstrel in.

Ring out false pride in place and blood,
　The civic slander and the spite;
　Ring in the love of truth and right,
Ring in the common love of good.

Ring out old shapes of foul disease;
　Ring out the narrowing lust of gold;
　Ring out the thousand wars of old,
Ring in the thousand years of peace.

Ring in the valiant man and free,
　The larger heart, the kindlier hand;
　Ring out the darkness of the land,
Ring in the Christ that is to be.

---

outputs.L2:
Sound out, untamed bells, into the untamed heavens,
Toward the drifting clouds and the cold, sharp glow:
Tonight the year breathes its last;
Sound out, untamed bells, and permit its passing.

Sound away the past, and welcome what is fresh,
Chime, joyful bells, over the blanket of snow:
The year departs, so let it take its leave;
Sound away deception, and welcome honesty.

Sound away the sorrow that drains our thoughts
For those we no longer find among us here;
Sound away the quarrel between wealthy and destitute,
And welcome justice for the whole human race.

Sound away a purpose that gradually fades,
Along with old traditions of political conflict;
Welcome the more dignified ways of living,
Accompanied by kinder customs and cleaner laws.

Sound away the poverty, the worry, the wrongdoing,
The unfaithful indifference of our age;
Sound away, sound away my sorrowful verses,
But welcome the richer poet within.

Sound away the false vanity of rank and lineage,
The slandering of communities and their malice;
Welcome the devotion to truth and what is just,
Welcome the shared affection for goodness.

Sound away the ancient forms of vile sickness;
Sound away the ever-tightening greed for wealth;
Sound away the countless conflicts of history,
And welcome a thousand years of tranquility.

Welcome the courageous and liberated man,
The more generous heart, the gentler hand;
Sound away the shadows covering the land,
And welcome the Christ who is yet to come.
outputs.L3:
# Ringing Out the Old, Ringing In the New

The poem opens with a stirring invocation, calling upon the wild bells to ring out across the sky and mark the passing of the dying old year while joyfully welcoming the arrival of the new one. In this moment of transition, the bells become powerful symbols of change and renewal, heralding both an ending and a fresh beginning.

Central to the poem's message is a passionate plea for moral and social transformation. The speaker urges the bells to ring out falsehood, grief, and the bitter feuds that divide the rich from the poor. In their place, the poem calls for the ringing in of truth and redress—a fairer, more just world in which all of mankind might find relief and reconciliation.

The speaker's vision extends to the political and cultural realms as well. There is a heartfelt desire to eliminate party strife and to sweep away the outdated forms of life that no longer serve humanity. These are to be replaced with nobler modes of living, sweeter manners, and purer laws—reflecting an aspiration toward a more refined and virtuous society.

Beyond these hopes, the poem seeks to banish the persistent ills that plague human existence. False pride, slander, greed, and disease are all to be cast out, making room for the enduring values of love, truth, and goodness to flourish in their stead. The bells thus serve as instruments not merely of celebration but of profound spiritual and ethical cleansing.

Ultimately, the poem builds toward a triumphant and redemptive vision. It calls for the ringing out of the darkness and wars of the past, longing instead to usher in a thousand years of peace. In its final and most exalted hope, the poem anticipates the coming of the Christ that is to be—a promise of ultimate goodness, harmony, and salvation for all the world.
outputs.L4:
# Tennyson's "Ring Out, Wild Bells": A Vision of Renewal

Alfred, Lord Tennyson's poem "Ring Out, Wild Bells" transforms the familiar sound of church bells tolling at midnight on New Year's Eve into a profound extended metaphor for change and renewal. Drawn from his larger elegiac work *In Memoriam*, the poem harnesses the traditional ringing of bells to mark the passing of the old year and the arrival of the new, giving this ceremonial moment a rich symbolic weight. The bells become more than an announcement of time's passage; they serve as a summons to transformation, both personal and universal.

The poem's structure is built upon a powerful rhetorical device: the repeated command to "ring out" what is old and corrupt and to "ring in" what is new and good. This anaphoric pattern gives the poem its driving momentum and its incantatory power. Each stanza issues its imperatives with increasing urgency, as though the poet were conducting the bells themselves, directing their peals toward a specific moral purpose. The repetition creates a sense of ritual, transforming the poem into something like a secular prayer or a chant for a better world.

Through this insistent structure, Tennyson catalogues the ills he hopes to banish from human experience. He calls upon the bells to ring out grief and sorrow, the personal pain that weighs upon the heart. He urges them to expel the social injustices that plague society—the "feud of rich and poor" and the inequalities that divide humanity. He seeks to drive away false pride, the narrow spite and ancient rivalries that poison human relationships. Disease and want, the physical sufferings of the body and the deprivations of poverty, are likewise to be cast off. Perhaps most emphatically, he demands an end to war itself, calling for the "thousand years of peace" that would mark a truly redeemed civilization.

Yet the poem is not merely a litany of complaint or a catalogue of what must be destroyed. For every evil to be rung out, Tennyson offers a corresponding good to be rung in. In place of grief and falsehood, he welcomes truth and honesty. In place of division and strife, he ushers in peace and fellowship among all people. He calls for the "larger heart, the kindlier hand," for a nobler and more generous humanity to emerge from the ashes of the old. The vision culminates in a longing for the coming of "the Christ that is to be"—a symbol of perfected human goodness and spiritual fulfillment.

In this way, the poem powerfully expresses a hopeful and forward-looking vision of transformation. Written during a period of both personal mourning and broad social change, "Ring Out, Wild Bells" moves beyond private grief toward a universal aspiration. Tennyson envisions humanity progressing steadily toward moral and spiritual improvement, leaving behind the corruptions and cruelties of the past. The poem ultimately affirms a faith in renewal—the belief that with each passing year, and with each ringing of the bells, the world may draw closer to a brighter and more compassionate future.

# The Perfect Ring

Choosing the right ring is one of the most meaningful decisions a person can make. Whether it symbolizes love, commitment, achievement, or simply personal style, a ring carries weight far beyond its physical size.

**The Meaning Behind the Ring**

For centuries, the ring has served as a powerful symbol across cultures. Its circular shape, with no beginning and no end, represents eternity and unbroken connection. This is why engagement rings and wedding bands remain such treasured traditions—they express a promise that is meant to last a lifetime.

**Finding the Ring for Every Occasion**

There is a ring for nearly every purpose:

- **For love:** Engagement and wedding rings mark the beginning of a shared journey.
- **For achievement:** Class rings and championship rings celebrate hard-earned success.
- **For style:** Fashion rings allow people to express their individuality and personality.
- **For heritage:** Family heirloom rings connect generations, passing stories from one hand to the next.

**Choosing the Right One**

When selecting a ring, consider the material, the fit, and the message you want it to convey. Gold, silver, and platinum each offer their own beauty, while gemstones add color and personal significance. The perfect ring is not always the most expensive—it is the one that feels right for the moment and the person wearing it.

In the end, the ring you choose becomes a small but lasting reminder of what matters most to you.

"Ring Out, Wild Bells" is a section (Canto 106) from Alfred, Lord Tennyson's larger work *In Memoriam A.H.H.* (1850). Here is the full text:

---

**Ring Out, Wild Bells**

Ring out, wild bells, to the wild sky,
    The flying cloud, the frosty light:
    The year is dying in the night;
Ring out, wild bells, and let him die.

Ring out the old, ring in the new,
    Ring, happy bells, across the snow:
    The year is going, let him go;
Ring out the false, ring in the true.

Ring out the grief that saps the mind,
    For those that here we see no more;
    Ring out the feud of rich and poor,
Ring in redress to all mankind.

Ring out a slowly dying cause,
    And ancient forms of party strife;
    Ring in the nobler modes of life,
With sweeter manners, purer laws.

Ring out the want, the care, the sin,
    The faithless coldness of the times;
    Ring out, ring out my mournful rhymes,
But ring the fuller minstrel in.

Ring out false pride in place and blood,
    The civic slander and the spite;
    Ring in the love of truth and right,
Ring in the common love of good.

Ring out old shapes of foul disease;
    Ring out the narrowing lust of gold;
    Ring out the thousand wars of old,
Ring in the thousand years of peace.

Ring in the valiant man and free,
    The larger heart, the kindlier hand;
    Ring out the darkness of the land,
Ring in the Christ that is to be.

---

This poem is often read or recited at New Year's celebrations because of its theme of ringing out the old year and welcoming the new.
